michelangelo-buonarroti.biography: Michelangelo was an Italian sculptor, painter, architect and poet. He trained in Florence and worked for popes in Rome. Alongside David and the Pietà, he made the Sistine Chapel ceiling and helped design St Peter’s Basilica.

jan-matejko.biography: Jan Matejko painted scenes from Polish history while the country was divided among neighboring powers. Working in Kraków, he used familiar historical figures to examine political responsibility, national achievements and the decisions behind Poland’s decline.

jacques-louis-david.biography: Jacques-Louis David was a French painter whose work helped define Neoclassicism. He painted ancient history and contemporary politics, supporting the French Revolution before becoming Napoleon’s official painter.

hans-holbein-the-younger.biography: Hans Holbein the Younger trained as a painter in Augsburg and worked in Basel before moving to England. His portraits recorded the merchants and courtiers of Tudor society. He also designed jewelry, metalwork and book illustrations.

francisco-goya.biography: Francisco Goya was a Spanish painter and printmaker who worked for the royal court. Alongside portraits and scenes of daily life, he depicted war, repression and superstition. His prints often addressed subjects that were difficult to confront in official commissions.

vincent-van-gogh.biography: Vincent van Gogh was a Dutch painter who began his artistic career as an adult. His early work focused on rural labor. In France, his palette became brighter and his brushwork more pronounced, shaping the portraits and landscapes for which he is best known.

jean-francois-millet.biography: Jean-François Millet grew up in rural Normandy and made agricultural work a major subject of his painting. His farm workers occupy the foreground rather than serving as background decoration. He settled in Barbizon, near the forest of Fontainebleau.

eugene-delacroix.biography: Eugène Delacroix was a French painter associated with Romanticism. He drew subjects from literature, contemporary events and his travels in North Africa. Strong color and animated figures distinguish his paintings, which include large public murals as well as easel works.

raphael.biography: Raphael trained in central Italy before working in Florence and Rome. Pope Julius II commissioned him to decorate rooms in the Vatican. Known for carefully organized figures and clear compositions, Raphael also worked as an architect, including at St Peter’s Basilica.

ludwig-van-beethoven.biography: Ludwig van Beethoven was born in Bonn and built his career as a pianist and composer in Vienna. His work expanded the scale and expressive range of the symphony, sonata and string quartet. He continued composing as his hearing deteriorated.

billie-holiday.biography: Billie Holiday was an American jazz singer known for her phrasing and sense of timing. She could reshape a familiar melody through small changes in rhythm and emphasis. Her repertoire included love songs as well as Strange Fruit, a protest against lynching.

joao-gilberto.biography: João Gilberto was a Brazilian singer and guitarist central to the emergence of bossa nova. His quiet singing and guitar rhythm brought a new intimacy to samba. His 1958 recording of Chega de Saudade helped establish the style.

george-orwell.biography: George Orwell was the pen name of Eric Arthur Blair, a British novelist, essayist and journalist. Experiences of poverty, imperial rule and the Spanish Civil War informed his writing. Animal Farm and Nineteen Eighty-Four examine political power and the manipulation of language.

graciliano-ramos.biography: Graciliano Ramos was a Brazilian novelist from Alagoas. His spare prose follows people constrained by poverty, authority and their difficulty expressing themselves. He also served as a mayor and wrote about his imprisonment under Getúlio Vargas in Memórias do Cárcere.

f-scott-fitzgerald.biography: F. Scott Fitzgerald was an American novelist and short-story writer closely associated with the 1920s. He wrote about ambition, wealth and the gap between public success and private disappointment. The Great Gatsby became his best-known novel.

michel-gondry.biography: Michel Gondry is a French filmmaker who began making music videos for his band Oui Oui. His films often use handmade sets, camera tricks and practical effects to represent imagination and memory. He directed Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind from Charlie Kaufman’s screenplay.

pete-docter-kemp-powers.biography: Pete Docter is a Pixar director whose films include Monsters, Inc., Up and Inside Out. Kemp Powers is a playwright and screenwriter whose work includes One Night in Miami. They co-wrote Soul, with Docter directing and Powers co-directing.

walter-salles.biography: Walter Salles is a Brazilian filmmaker whose work often follows people through journeys and social change. He directed Central Station and The Motorcycle Diaries. In I’m Still Here, he returned to Brazil’s military dictatorship through the experience of the Paiva family.

pantheon-architect-unknown.biography: The architect of the surviving Pantheon is unknown. The building was completed during the reign of the Roman emperor Hadrian, drawing on Roman builders’ experience with concrete vaults and large public spaces.

theodore-gericault.biography: Théodore Géricault was a French painter associated with Romanticism. In The Raft of the Medusa, he gave a recent shipwreck the scale usually reserved for major historical subjects. He studied survivors and human bodies while preparing the painting, which he exhibited in Paris in 1819.

diego-velazquez.biography: Diego Velázquez trained in Seville before becoming a painter at the court of Philip IV in Madrid. His portraits include the royal family, courtiers and people who served the palace. In Las Meninas, he also placed himself at work inside the royal household.

jan-van-eyck.biography: Jan van Eyck painted religious works and portraits for courtiers, churchmen and merchants. He worked for Philip the Good, Duke of Burgundy, and used thin layers of oil paint to describe light and surfaces with unusual precision. His surviving signed paintings include The Arnolfini Portrait.

winslow-homer.biography: Winslow Homer began his career as an illustrator and reported on the American Civil War through drawings. He later painted rural life and coastal communities, working in both oils and watercolors. His journeys to the Caribbean expanded the settings and subjects of his seascapes.

gustave-caillebotte.biography: Gustave Caillebotte painted everyday life in Paris, including its workers, streets and newly built neighborhoods. He also supported fellow Impressionists by buying their paintings. His bequest to the French state helped bring works by artists including Monet, Renoir and Degas into the national collection.

diego-rivera.biography: Diego Rivera was a Mexican painter who made large public murals about history, work and political conflict. After studying European painting, he returned to Mexico and helped develop its mural movement. His images brought workers and Indigenous histories into prominent civic spaces.

candido-portinari.biography: Candido Portinari grew up near Brodowski, São Paulo, in a family of Italian immigrants who worked on a coffee plantation. He painted rural workers, migrants and childhood scenes, bringing Brazilian social life into modern painting. His public commissions include the War and Peace panels at the United Nations.

johannes-vermeer.biography: Johannes Vermeer lived and worked in Delft in the Dutch Republic. His paintings often show people reading, making music or working in quiet rooms. Careful attention to light and everyday objects gives these small domestic scenes much of their character. Only about 35 paintings are generally accepted as his work.

caravaggio.biography: Michelangelo Merisi, known as Caravaggio, built his career in Rome after training in northern Italy. He brought religious stories close to everyday life, giving saints the appearance of ordinary people. His strong contrasts of light and shadow influenced painters across Europe.

tarsila-do-amaral.biography: Tarsila do Amaral helped develop modern painting in Brazil while moving between São Paulo and Paris. She combined lessons from Cubism with Brazilian landscapes, people and popular culture. Her painting Abaporu inspired the idea that Brazilian artists could absorb foreign influences and turn them into something of their own.

john-everett-millais.biography: John Everett Millais entered the Royal Academy Schools as a child and helped found the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood in 1848. His early paintings gave literary and religious subjects sharply observed detail. Later, he became a successful portrait painter and served briefly as president of the Royal Academy.

john-constable.biography: John Constable made the Suffolk countryside where he grew up a central subject of his painting. He studied changing skies and rural scenes outdoors, then developed large exhibition paintings in his studio. His landscapes became especially influential in France, where The Hay Wain won a gold medal in 1824.

j-m-w-turner.biography: J. M. W. Turner was a British painter whose landscapes and seascapes explored light, weather and human activity. His subjects ranged from ancient history to steamships, railways and the slave trade. He worked in both oil and watercolor, often allowing atmosphere to soften the outlines of objects.

ilya-repin.biography: Born in what is now Ukraine, Ilya Repin built his career in the Russian Empire. He painted workers, political events and portraits with close attention to individual people. Barge Haulers on the Volga helped establish his reputation; later, he lived and worked in Kuokkala, then part of Finland.

moche-artists.biography: The maker of this vessel is not known by name. Moche artists on Peru’s north coast modeled ceramic vessels as people, animals and scenes of ritual life. Their portrait bottles preserve recognizable faces within a tradition that linked skilled craft with social standing and ceremonial use.

nasca-artists.biography: The maker of this bottle is not known by name. Nasca artists on Peru’s south coast made pottery with vivid painted surfaces, combining animals, plants and supernatural figures. Such vessels formed part of feasting and funerary practices as well as the region’s wider visual culture.

sam-cooke.biography: Sam Cooke began as a gospel singer before becoming a leading figure in soul music. Born in Mississippi and raised in Chicago, he brought a smooth, expressive voice to both love songs and songs about public life. A Change Is Gonna Come became closely associated with the civil rights movement.

chico-buarque.biography: Chico Buarque is a Brazilian songwriter, singer, playwright and novelist. His songs often speak through invented characters, using their daily lives to explore love, work and social inequality. During Brazil’s military dictatorship, he also wrote songs that challenged political repression.

franz-kafka.biography: Franz Kafka wrote in German while working in insurance in Prague. He published only a small part of his work during his lifetime and was deeply critical of his own writing. His friend Max Brod preserved and published many manuscripts after Kafka’s death, despite instructions to destroy them.
